payload.rationale:
The supplied CDC report gives 3,471 confirmed U.S. cases through September 17. Strictly exceeding 6,000 requires at least 2,530 additional cases in the count recognized under the contract. Over roughly 105 remaining days, that means about 169 cases per week, versus approximately 93 per week averaged so far. A simple continuation of the year-to-date average would finish near 4,900; this is a benchmark, not an estimate of the current transmission rate.

I assign a 25% chance because reaching the threshold requires substantially higher remaining-year incidence than the year-to-date average, but measles outbreaks can produce rapid, uneven increases. The reported 39 new outbreaks and 95% outbreak-associated share support substantial uncertainty rather than a smooth extrapolation. The 2025 total of 2,289 provides context but does not establish the 2026 trajectory.

The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is that existing outbreaks may already be declining through containment or depletion of susceptible contacts; without weekly data, sustained transmission could be overstated. The strongest reason it could be too low is that incidence may already be accelerating, with school-linked spread or introductions into undervaccinated communities capable of generating several thousand additional cases. These are transfer assumptions, not observed current trends. Reporting delays also matter because revisions after expiration do not count.
limitations: No weekly incidence series, recent growth rate, outbreak sizes, geographic distribution, or susceptible-population estimates are supplied.
The probability is a judgmental estimate, not the output of a fitted transmission model.
CDC counts are provisional and assigned by epidemiological week of rash onset; reporting timing and the exclusion of post-expiration revisions can affect settlement.
The supplied evidence packet is small and was not independently verified.
